provenance.notes:
Debian slim images ship no man pages, so the flag list was read from GNU --help, which is complete by GNU convention -- EXCEPT that it is not, here, and the exceptions are recorded below. `strings` is absent from the image, so the option table was interrogated through getopt_long's own behaviour instead.

TWO REAL OPTIONS ARE MISSING FROM --help: `--binary` and `--zero-terminated`. Both are accepted (exit 0) while a genuinely bogus `--bogus` is rejected with `sed: unrecognized option '--bogus'`, so the acceptance is not a blanket one. They are registered options, not typos tolerated by chance: getopt_long resolves unambiguous prefixes only against the real option table, and `--bin` and `--binar` are both accepted, as are `--zero` and `--zero-term`. The table was read back directly from the ambiguity diagnostic -- `sed --s` reports `option '--s' is ambiguous; possibilities: '--silent' '--sandbox' '--separate'`. `--binary` has no observable effect on Linux (`sed --binary 's/a/X/'` on a CRLF file produces byte-identical output to plain sed); it exists for platforms that distinguish text and binary streams. `--zero-terminated` is a second long spelling of -z, whose only documented long form is --null-data. Under `authoritative` a help-only transcription would have erased both.

-i TAKES AN OPTIONAL SUFFIX THAT MUST BE ATTACHED, WHICH IS THE MIRROR IMAGE OF THE BSD TRAP. --help spells it `-i[SUFFIX], --in-place[=SUFFIX]`, so value_optional is set. `sed -i 's/a/X/' t1.txt` works and edits in place with no backup. `sed -i.bak 's/a/X/' t2.txt` works and writes t2.txt.bak. But `sed -i .bak 's/a/X/' t3.txt` fails with `sed: -e expression #1, char 1: unknown command: '.'` (exit 1, file unmodified), because the separated `.bak` is read as the script. `--in-place=.bk` succeeds and `--in-place .bk` fails the same way. Where BSD requires the operand and GNU forbids separating it, the attached form `-i.bak` is the only spelling that works on both.

-l MEANS SOMETHING ELSE HERE THAN IT DOES ON BSD. GNU -l/--line-length takes N and sets the wrap width for the `l` command (`sed -n -l 2 l` on `aaaa` prints `a\`/`a\`/`a\`/`a$`); BSD -l is a boolean meaning line-buffered output. Same letter, unrelated behaviour, so no description may be copied between the two files.

-i IMPLIES -s. Probed with A.txt=`1\n2\n`, B.txt=`3\n4\n`: `sed -n '$p' A.txt B.txt` prints `4` (one continuous stream), while `sed -i -n '$p' A.txt B.txt` leaves A=`2` and B=`4`, the same per-file result as -s alone. They are therefore not conflicting -- one subsumes the other.

--sandbox DISABLES e/r/w BUT NOT IN-PLACE EDITING. `sed --sandbox 's/z/x/w w2.out' in.txt` is refused with `e/r/w commands disabled in sandbox mode` (exit 1) and leaves the target file intact, but `sed --sandbox -i 's/a/X/' s.txt` still rewrites s.txt (exit 0). It is the right flag to require when a script comes from an untrusted source, and it is not a substitute for withholding -i.

THE `w` FUNCTION TRUNCATES ITS TARGET BEFORE ANY INPUT IS READ, exactly as on BSD, and GNU has no -a to delay it. With w.out containing `PRECIOUS`, `sed 's/nomatch/x/w w.out' in.txt` exits 0 having matched nothing and leaves w.out empty. This is why the command is annotated destructive independently of -i.

NO MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE PAIR WAS FOUND, so conflicts_with is empty throughout -- deliberately, not by omission. GNU sed has no -I, so the BSD -I/-i override does not arise here. The repeated-spelling groups are aliases rather than conflicts and are accepted together: `sed -n --quiet --silent p` and `sed -E -r 's/a+/X/'` both exit 0.

END-OF-OPTIONS: `sed -- 's/a/X/' ./-w.txt` is accepted (exit 0), so end_of_options is true.

GRAMMAR, quoting --help verbatim: "If no -e, --expression, -f, or --file option is given, then the first non-option argument is taken as the sed script to interpret." Probed: `sed -e 's/a/X/' 's/a/Y/' g.txt` reports `sed: can't read s/a/Y/: No such file or directory` and exits 2.

THE LONG-OPTION TABLE WAS ENUMERATED, NOT TRANSCRIBED, so `authoritative` rests on a closure proof rather than on trusting --help. getopt_long resolves an unambiguous prefix and names the candidates for an ambiguous one, so `sed --<letter>` classifies each initial letter. Sweeping a-z against this build: b d e h i l n p q r u v z each resolve to exactly one option; f reports `'--file' '--follow-symlinks'` and s reports `'--silent' '--sandbox' '--separate'`; and a c g j k m o t w x y are all `unrecognized option`. That is 18 long options, which is exactly the 18 this overlay carries, with the per-letter counts matching one for one. No long option exists that is not listed here, and none listed here is absent from the binary.

ONE FALSE ACCUSATION WAS RAISED AND DISMISSED DURING THE CHECK, recorded because the next auditor will hit it too. A sweep that fed every flag through `printf 'a\n' | sed <flag> 's/a/X/'` reported -i and --in-place as REJECTED. The binary is fine; the harness was wrong. In-place editing needs a file operand, and with stdin alone sed correctly answers `sed: no input files`. Re-run against a real file, `sed -i 's/a/X/' i1.txt` and `sed --in-place 's/a/X/' i2.txt` both exit 0 and leave `X`.

SECOND INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION ON A DIFFERENT BUILD, PLATFORM AND VERSION. Everything above was re-run against Homebrew's GNU sed 4.10 on macOS 26.5.2 (/opt/homebrew/opt/gnu-sed/libexec/gnubin/sed, `brew install gnu-sed`), and the option table is identical to Debian's 4.9: the same fifteen initial letters answer, f still reports `'--file' '--follow-symlinks'` and s still reports `'--silent' '--sandbox' '--separate'`, the same eleven letters are unrecognized, and diffing 4.10's --help against this overlay's long options is empty in the erasure direction. Nothing was added between 4.9 and 4.10 that an authoritative overlay written against 4.9 would erase. `--binary` and `--zero-terminated` are accepted by 4.10 too and are still absent from its --help, so their omission is systematic rather than a Debian packaging artifact. The behavioural claims reproduce unchanged: `-i .bak` separated fails with `unknown command: '.'` leaving the file untouched while `-i.bak` attached succeeds and writes the backup; a `w` target containing `PRECIOUS` is left empty by a script that matches nothing; --sandbox refuses the w command while still allowing -i to rewrite the file; and -i alone reproduces -s's per-file `$` address.

NO version_range IS SET, deliberately. Two releases now agree on the whole option set, so a pin would only turn a future 4.11 into an unmatched overlay -- which under authoritative mode silently falls back to a heuristic scan rather than failing loudly. checked_on plus re-verification is the intended control here, not a version constraint.

open_world IS SET TRUE, AND THIS IS THE FIELD THE NAME LISTS CANNOT REACH. GNU sed's `e` flag on a substitution runs the replacement as a shell command: `printf 'x\n' | sed 's/x/echo PWNED/e'` prints `PWNED` (exit 0). The same script under --sandbox is refused with `e/r/w commands disabled in sandbox mode`. `sed` is on neither OPEN_WORLD_TOOLS nor EXEC_WRAPPER_TOOLS, so inference calls it closed-world -- correct for BSD sed, wrong here. Nothing about the string "sed" can distinguish the two, which is why this has to be asserted per variant.

description: Stream editor. Reads the specified files, or standard input if none are given, applies a script of editing commands to each line, and writes the result to standard output. If no -e or -f option is given, the first non-option argument is taken as the script and all remaining arguments are input files. With -i the files are edited in place instead, and the `w` function writes to named files whether or not in-place editing is on.

flags.description: Suppress automatic printing of pattern space.
Suppress automatic printing of pattern space; listed by --help as a second long spelling of -n/--quiet.
Annotate program execution, printing the parsed program and then the input line, pattern space and command for each cycle.
Add the script to the commands to be executed.
Add the contents of script-file to the commands to be executed.
Follow symlinks when processing in place.
Edit files in place, making a backup if SUFFIX is supplied. The suffix must be attached (-iSUFFIX or --in-place=SUFFIX); a separated value is read as the script instead. Implies --separate.
Specify the desired line-wrap length for the `l' command. This is not the BSD -l, which is a boolean selecting line-buffered output.
Use extended regular expressions in the script. For portability use POSIX -E.
Use extended regular expressions in the script; listed by --help as a second short spelling of -E/--regexp-extended.
Consider files as separate rather than as a single, continuous long stream.
Operate in sandbox mode, disabling the e/r/w commands. It does not disable in-place editing.
Load minimal amounts of data from the input files and flush the output buffers more often.
Separate lines by NUL characters; a second long spelling of -z that the binary accepts but --help does not list.
Open files in binary mode on platforms that distinguish text and binary streams. Accepted by the binary but shown nowhere in --help, and without observable effect on Linux.
Display a usage message and exit.

positional_args.name: script
positional_args.description: The sed script, taken from the first non-option argument only when no -e, --expression, -f or --file option is given. If any is present this slot does not exist and every operand is an input file.

positional_args.name: input-file
positional_args.description: Input files. With none, standard input is read. With -i these files are rewritten in place.
